sections.h2: Ways to sell a house fast in Minneapolis
sections.html:
You can list with an agent, sell on your own, or sell directly to a cash buyer. Whichever route you take, a house, duplex or townhouse in the city needs a Truth in Sale of Housing report before anyone can be shown through it, so that step shapes your schedule more than the choice of buyer does.

Minneapolis has 430,324 residents on 54 square miles of land. Owners live in 47.7 percent of homes, so plenty of houses change hands between investors, landlords and first-time buyers as well as long-term owners. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $362,200, rent is $1,371 and owners with a mortgage pay a median $2,128 a month, across 192,734 households. The average commute is 22.0 minutes. A bungalow near a lake and a duplex on a busy corridor can sit far from those middle figures, so treat them as context and not as an appraisal.

  • Agent listing: the widest exposure, though showings wait for the city report to be filed and displayed.
  • Sale by owner: the same city report applies, and you handle disclosures and paperwork yourself.
  • Cash sale: the buyer takes the house in its present condition, and the report still has to exist for the transfer.

sections.h2: The Truth in Sale report before showings
sections.html:
The city requires a Truth in Sale of Housing (TISH) evaluation for single-family houses, duplexes, townhouses and first-time condominium conversions, and the full report must exist before you show the property. It applies to sales by owner, sales through an agent, advertising a home for sale, contracts for deed and other title transfers. The city's TISH page explains the program.

You hire an evaluator approved by Minneapolis. Evaluators are not city employees and set their own prices, so comparing quotes is reasonable. The evaluator inspects the building inside and outside, writes the disclosure report and files it online where you and the city can both see it.

A report stays valid for two years or one sale, whichever ends first. Keep a copy on display so prospective buyers can read it at showings. A separate pre-inspection report does not replace it.

Two situations skip the evaluation: a property holding a Certificate of Code Compliance (issued when a house comes out of condemnation, good for up to one year) or a Certificate of Occupancy for a newly built home (good for one sale).

When the evaluator lists required repairs, you can complete them and receive a Certificate of Approval online, or sell with the repairs open and pass them to the buyer. If the work is still undone at closing, the buyer signs an acknowledgement of responsibility, and the city asks for that form within one business day of closing. The buyer then has 90 days after closing to finish the repairs.

Open repairs on a Minneapolis TISH report
SituationPaperworkWho finishes the work
Seller finishes all repairsCertificate of ApprovalSeller, before the sale

Before you book the evaluation, review the city's list of commonly required repairs and fix what you can, since fixed items will not appear on the report. After the buyer completes the work, an evaluator or a city inspector reinspects, and a successful result brings a Certificate of Completion.

For a seller with a dated house, this is the main cost question. Minneapolis Truth in Housing is reachable at 612-673-5840.

sections.h2: How Hennepin County taxes affect your sale
sections.html:
Hennepin County collects Minneapolis property tax in two halves, due May 15 and October 15. A 15th that falls on a non-business day slides to the next business day. Statements and valuation notices arrive in March, and the valuation shows how the property was assessed as of January 2.

That timing matters when you sell. A summer sale leaves the second-half bill still ahead, and the assessment you see in March sets next year's tax. Your share depends on the assessor's value, how the property is classified and the levies of the taxing districts that cover it, and more than 70 local governments levy in the county. The county's property tax line is 612-348-3011.

Your purchase agreement decides who covers the current year's bill, so ask the title company how it will be apportioned.

Minnesota law requires a written seller disclosure before you sign a purchase agreement. Under Minnesota Statutes 513.55, you list material facts you know that could significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment, and the disclosure must be made in good faith. A leaking basement, a past sewer backup or an unpermitted addition belongs there.

The city's 2040 Comprehensive Plan ended single-family-only zoning citywide. A buyer evaluating your lot may ask what the zoning would allow, so ask the city's planning staff before you answer.

Winter timing is real. Summers run hot and humid and winters bring heavy snow, so exterior photos, roof condition and drainage are easier to show in spring and fall. The city has 83 neighborhoods, and buyers often search by neighborhood and by distance to light rail, which the Metro Blue and Green lines provide.

sections.h2: When a cash sale makes sense
sections.html:
A cash sale tends to suit owners facing a deadline, an inherited house, tenants who will not leave, or repairs that a TISH report would make visible. The buyer purchases the house as it stands, and the open repair items move to the new owner through the acknowledgement process.

Compare any offer to what the same house would net after listing costs, a repair list and carrying costs while it sits. Ask who pays for the evaluation, how the buyer handles the city paperwork and when funds arrive. You can also request a written offer with no obligation and a firm closing date.

sections.h2: Getting ready before the evaluator arrives
sections.html: Clear access to the basement, attic, furnace, water heater and electrical panel, and unlock any outbuildings. Replace burned-out bulbs, fix loose handrails and test the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, since small items like these often appear on a report. Gather permits for past work and any receipts for repairs. Keep the evaluation, the disclosure and your tax statement in one folder, so you can hand each to the buyer or title company without a search.

faqs.q: Do I need a Truth in Sale of Housing report to sell my Minneapolis house?
faqs.a: Yes for most houses. Single-family houses, duplexes, townhouses and first-time condominium conversions need the report before the property is shown. A Certificate of Code Compliance or a Certificate of Occupancy for a new build can replace it.

faqs.q: How long is a Minneapolis TISH report good for?
faqs.a: Two years or one sale, whichever comes first. A buyer who finishes any open repairs must obtain a new report before reselling.

faqs.q: Who pays for repairs listed on the city report?
faqs.a: The purchase agreement decides. If repairs remain open at closing, the buyer signs an acknowledgement of responsibility, files it within one business day, and finishes the work within 90 days.

faqs.q: What dates does Hennepin County set for Minneapolis property tax?
faqs.a: May 15 and October 15. When either lands on a weekend or holiday, you have until the next business day.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Minneapolis house that needs major repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. The report must still be filed and displayed, but you are allowed to sell with required repairs outstanding if the buyer accepts them and signs the acknowledgement. A cash buyer often takes that route.
